titulo: Square desktop robot: rotating and tilting screen head, to print on the A1 — robos-impressos
meta: 20 cm square desktop robot with a screen on its face and a head that rotates and tilts. STL and 3MF files are already positioned for printing, with a shopping list that includes estimated prices and links, step-by-step assembly instructions, and a wire-by-wire wiring diagram.
hero_h1: Square desktop robot: rotating and tilting screen head, for you to print on the A1
hero_lead: You want a robot on your desk and don't want to get stuck halfway through: a screw is missing, a part doesn't fit in the printer, and nobody tells you what to buy or where each wire goes. Here, the files are already in print position, the list tells you what the robot uses and how much to buy, and the assembly takes you from the first threaded insert to the last wire.
hero_fase: Phase 1 = body assembled and wired. The program (face on the screen, voice, camera) comes later, in phase 2.
hero_alt: Render of the square desktop robot: a white cube head with a dark panel and a screen showing two eyes, on top of a low gray base
hero_cap: Render of the actual model, the same one used to generate the print files. The screen shows the face the robot will display in phase 2.
resumo: The square robot is a [[N_ALTURA]] cm desktop robot that you can print at home and assemble. Its head is a cube with a 3.5-inch screen on its face; it rotates almost all the way around and tilts up and down. Inside are a Raspberry Pi, an Arduino, two servos, and a battery that charges via USB-C. You need a 3D printer with a 256 mm build plate, the parts on the shopping list, and a soldering iron. This page covers phase 1: the body assembled, the wires connected, and both servos centered. Programming (screen face, voice, camera, AI) is phase 2 and has not been done yet.

mon_sub: First, three prep steps on the workbench, with the parts still loose. Then assembly, in the same order the checker tested: each part goes in from the indicated side without hitting anything already assembled.
prep_t: Before assembly: 3 prep steps on the workbench
prep_p: These steps come first because once the robot is closed up, you can’t reach the converter adjustment, the Arduino USB port, or the Raspberry Pi card. Prep steps 1 and 2 are electrical and have not been bench-tested: measure every connection with a multimeter before turning on the switch.
prep1_t: Wire the power and set both voltages
prep1_p: Assemble the wiring harness on the workbench, following the wiring diagram: battery holder, fuse, protection board, charger, switch, LM2596 converter, and UBEC. Use the printed base next to it as a guide for wire lengths. Don't connect the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, or servos yet. Turn on the switch and, using a multimeter, turn the LM2596 adjustment screw until the output reads 5,1 V; check that the UBEC output reads 6 V (its jumper set to 6 V). Turn it off.
prep2_t: Upload the program to the Arduino and set both servos to 90°
prep2_p: Open the sketch centrar_servos.ino in the Arduino IDE, connect the Uno to the computer with the USB cable (without the shield or battery), select the Arduino Uno board, and click Upload. Unplug the USB cable, fit the Sensor Shield onto the Uno, and remove the SEL jumper from the shield. Plug the USB cable back in, just to measure: the shield’s 5 V pin should read about 5 V, and the D9 V pin should read 0 V. Unplug the USB cable. Now connect the UBEC’s 6 V to the blue screw terminal, the LM2596’s 5.1 V to the shield’s 5 V pin, the pan servo to D9, and the tilt servo to D10. Turn on the switch: both servos will move to the center (90°), and the Uno LED will blink. Turn it off, and don’t turn the shafts by hand again. Don’t power the MG996R through USB: it supplies 0.5 A, and the servo draws more when starting.
prep3_t: Flash the Raspberry Pi microSD card
prep3_p: Use Raspberry Pi Imager, the free Raspberry Pi program: choose your Pi model, the Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit) system, and the card. Before flashing, open Imager settings and set a username, password, and Wi-Fi, and enable SSH: this lets you access the Pi over the network without a keyboard. The MPI3501 screen (ILI9486 controller, connected over SPI) only turns on after you install the driver. The manufacturer recommends the LCD-show package: git clone https://github.com/goodtft/LCD-show.git, then cd LCD-show and sudo ./LCD35-show (source: lcdwiki.com, MPI3501 page). The script replaces the Pi's configuration file and restarts it. Not bench-tested: the manufacturer lists tests up to the Raspberry Pi 3B+; the Pi 4 and Pi 5 may need adjustments.
prep_nota: Threaded inserts: set the iron between 220 and 250 °C, a little above the printing temperature for the part's plastic (typical value, NC). Place the tip inside the insert, let the heat soften the plastic, and slowly push without forcing it until the insert is flush with the surface. If your iron has no temperature control, apply heat for less time.
mon_paraf_t: Screws and inserts, one by one
mon_paraf_p: There are [[N_INSERTOS]] M3 heat-set inserts. Seat them all before you start assembling.
mon_passos_p: Steps marked (workbench) are done outside the robot, with the part in your hand.
mon_abrir_p: Replacing the battery or working on the boards does not require disassembling the head.
en_sub: Two 18650 batteries in series provide 6 to 8,4 V. From there, two separate lines supply 5,1 V to the Raspberry Pi and Arduino, and 6 V to the servos.
seg_li:
• None of this has been bench-tested. The diagram is based on the component datasheets. Check every connection with a multimeter before turning on the switch.
  • Polarity: red to positive, black to negative. Measure before each new connection. Reversed wiring burns out the board immediately.
  • Adjust before connecting the load: set the LM2596 to 5,1 V and the UBEC to 6 V, measured with a multimeter, with the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, and servos disconnected.
  • A short circuit can start a fire: solder with the cells OUT of the holder and insulate each joint with heat-shrink tubing. The 5 A fuse goes right after the holder.
  • Matching cells: use two new 18650 cells of the same brand and model. A dented, swollen, or hot cell goes to battery recycling, not into the robot.
  • First charge: stay nearby, with the robot on a nonflammable surface.
en_f3: LM2596: 5,1 V for the Raspberry Pi and Arduino · UBEC: 6 V for the 2 servos
en1_t: 5,1 V for the Raspberry Pi and Arduino
en1_p: The LM2596 converter keeps the voltage at 5 V until the battery drops to about 6,5 V. One pair of wires runs up through the neck to the Pi's USB-C adapter; another pair goes to the Sensor Shield's 5 V pin. It supplies up to 3 A: use a Pi 4, or a Pi 5 without power-hungry USB accessories.
en2_p: The UBEC supplies 3 A continuously to both MG996R servos through the Sensor Shield's blue screw terminal, with the SEL jumper removed. If the jumper were in place, the 6 V would flow into the Arduino's 5 V line. A 1000 µF capacitor at the terminal helps handle the startup surge.
en3_p: The balance charger sits with its port at a window behind the base and accepts a USB-C power supply up to 15 W. It needs a third wire, soldered to the point joining the two cells. It connects before the switch, so the robot charges while switched off.
en4_t: The Raspberry Pi and Arduino communicate over serial
en4_p: The Pi is in the head and the Arduino is in the base, and a USB plug won't fit through the 9 mm hole in the neck. So they connect over a 3-wire serial (UART) connection: the Pi transmits through pin 32 and listens through pin 33. The Arduino runs at 5 V and the Pi at 3,3 V: three 1 kΩ resistors lower the voltage on the wire from the Arduino to the Pi.
esq_p: Each box is a component, and each line is a wire in the indicated color. Click to open it at full size.
esq_img_alt: Wiring diagram: battery, fuse, protection board, charger, switch, converters, Arduino with Sensor Shield, servos, Raspberry Pi, and screen, with colored wires connecting them
lig_p: The same information as the diagram, with one line per wire. Names in parentheses are the ones usually printed on the boards; if your board uses a different name, follow the name on the board.
en_nota: Calculated current, not measured: under normal use, the battery pack supplies about 2 A. In the worst case (both converters at their limit with a low battery), it would be about 6 A, above the fuse rating. That's why the phase 2 program must not let both servos strain at the same time.

ver_ok_li:
• Each STL is a closed mesh and fits on the 256 mm build plate.
  • No part passes through another part or component in 10 head positions.
  • Each part goes in and comes out through the side indicated in the assembly instructions.
  • The robot doesn’t tip over with the head at either extreme.
  • No part needs supports in the file’s print position.
ver_nao_t: What only printing can tell you
ver_nao_li:
• The actual clearances on your printer: that’s why the test part comes first.
  • The dimensions marked NC on the purchased components.
  • The actual time and weight: the numbers are estimates without a slicer.
  • The strength of the gears and fork in use.
  • The electrical section: the wiring diagram was based on the component datasheets and has not been bench-tested.
